query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The corrosion behavior of pre‐exposed Q235 steel is primarily dictated by the integrity and composition of its naturally formed passive oxide film. A continuous, defect‐free oxide layer suppresses localized corrosion by impeding ion and electron transfer, while defects or discontinuities in this film serve as initiation sites for accelerated corrosion—effects that become more pronounced at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 mild steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state with its native thin passive oxide (mainly Fe2O3/Fe3O4) film intact.
generation.intervention: Deliberately modify the surface oxide integrity by (a) mechanical abrasion to introduce controlled defects, and (b) chemical passivation (or mild annealing) to enhance oxide uniformity.
generation.conditions: Exposure tests in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous solution) conducted at room temperature (~25°C) and an elevated temperature (e.g., 70°C) under controlled immersion and potential cycling conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The native passive oxide layer on Q235 steel, with its defect density and chemical composition.
generation.mechanism: A uniform, defect‐free oxide film limits corrosive ion access and electron exchange, thereby suppressing anodic iron dissolution. In contrast, film discontinuities or defects create localized anodic sites that accelerate corrosion through preferential dissolution. This mechanism is further amplified at higher temperatures due to increased reaction rates and ion mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples with an intact, uniform oxide film will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates and fewer pitting sites than samples with deliberately introduced surface defects; the difference in degradation behavior is predicted to be more marked at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Corrosion performance (via electrochemical and weight loss measures) of untreated Q235 steel with its normal, as-formed passive film under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to pre-exposed Q235 steel where the chemical composition of the substrate is constant and no additional corrosion inhibitors or surface coatings are present. It assumes that any observed differences in corrosion are predominantly due to variations in the oxide film’s integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between defect density in the oxide film and corrosion rate is not fully delineated, and the temperature threshold at which oxide film breakdown accelerates may vary with subtle changes in environmental chemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Q235 steel samples: one set left as received (intact oxide layer), one subjected to controlled mechanical abrasion (to disrupt the oxide film), and a third set that is first abraded, then chemically passivated to re-establish a uniform oxide layer. Expose all sets to a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at both room temperature and 70°C under identical cycling conditions. Monitor the corrosion behavior over a fixed period.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization to assess corrosion current density and potential
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to evaluate passive film integrity
Surface imaging (optical/SEM) for pitting density and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically abraded samples (with disrupted oxide films) do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in corrosion rates, pitting density, or changes in electrochemical parameters compared to the as-received and re-passivated samples under both temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that the oxide film integrity governs corrosion onset would be falsified.

Effect of ZrC on the Microstructure and Properties of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Prepared by a Plasma Transferred Arc Process

Abstract: The low strength caused by the single FCC structure of the CrMnFeCoNi high entropy alloy (HEA) limits its application in the field of coating. Here, we prepared high-entropy alloy coatings of CrMnFeCoNi with different ZrC contents on Q235 steel by a plasma transferred arc process. The effects of ZrC on the microstructure and properties of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating were investigated by optical microscopy, scanning electron microscope, and X-ray diffraction and by employing a potensiostat/galvanostat. The results showed that ZrC mainly existed in the coatings as a second phase, having little influence on the main crystal structure and micromorphology of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating. The hardness of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increased with the ZrC content. ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating. In a 1 mol/L NaCl solution with 4 wt% ZrC, the annual corrosion rate was only 5.997% of that of the HEA coating.
